item.mechanism: The Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) process induces the formation of a secondary Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase from the original Body Centered Cubic (BCC) solid solution during the slow cooling phase following the heat treatment.
item.system: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy (both gravity-cast and suction-assisted cast variants)
item.operating_conditions: HIP at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h, followed by slow cooling inside the furnace
item.supporting_observation: XRD and SEM analysis confirmed the presence of two phases (BCC and HCP) only after HIP, whereas as-cast samples were single-phase BCC.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold for as-cast material due to rapid cooling which results in a supercooled BCC phase; the specific mechanism (eutectoid vs. precipitation) requires further confirmation.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that previous literature (Senkov et al.) suggested the BCC phase might be metastable but did not detect the HCP peaks observed here.
quotes: It seems that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of the HCP phase mentioned above.

It is therefore reasonable to derive that when the HIP process of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy ends and the alloy is left to cool at a very slow rate inside the furnace the HCP phase forms out of the original BCC phase, either by a eutectoid reaction or by precipitation.
An HCP phase is not created in the case of the as-cast alloy due to the rapid cooling, resulting in a supercooled BCC phase.

item.mechanism: The appearance of the secondary HCP phase increases material hardness by impeding dislocation mobility, functioning similarly to precipitation hardening.
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature hardness testing on HIP-processed specimens
item.supporting_observation: Hardness increased significantly after HIP (e.g., from ~323 HV to 437 HV for gravity cast), correlating with the appearance of the HCP phase.
item.scope_limits: The magnitude of hardness increase depends on the distribution of the HCP phase; suction-assisted casting showed higher hardness due to grain boundary concentration.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated, but the authors attribute the increase specifically to the HCP phase presence.
quotes: The hardness increase after HIP can be related to the appearance of the secondary HCP phase and its influence on dislocation mobility, similarly to precipitation hardening.

The difference between the suction-assisted cast and the gravity cast may be related to the distribution of the ZrHf-rich phase, which is evenly dispersed in the case of the gravity casting while concentrated mainly at the grain boundaries in the case of the suction-assisted casting.

item.mechanism: The material exhibits extreme brittleness under tensile loading due to the lack of plastic deformation mechanisms, leading to inter-crystalline fracture.
item.system: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy (gravity-cast and suction-assisted cast, HIP-processed)
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature tension tests and creep tests at 982 °C under 120 MPa and 200 MPa
item.supporting_observation: Fractography showed inter-crystalline fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation; elongation to fracture was below machine detection limits.
item.scope_limits: This brittle behavior is specific to tension; the material shows high ductility (>50% strain) and higher strength under compression.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that cold-rolled and annealed versions of the alloy showed ductility, implying the as-cast/HIP microstructure is the cause of brittleness.
quotes: Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C.
The figures show that the fracture is inter-crystalline in both cases, without any plastic deformation.

These poor results under tension load lead to the conclusion that the material is extremely brittle and therefore cannot withstand any tension stress applied either at room temperature or at high temperatures.

item.mechanism: Oxidation and pre-existing surface cracks contribute to premature failure during high-temperature creep under tension.
item.supporting_observation: EDS analysis revealed high concentrations of oxidation products near the surface of broken creep specimens, suggesting cracks allowed oxidation to penetrate.
item.scope_limits: The exact propagation process of these cracks and their specific influence on failure is not fully characterized and requires further investigation.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors suggest the oxidation is a consequence of pre-existing cracks rather than the sole initiation cause.
quotes: The high concentration of oxides beneath the surface detected in the broken creep specimens may be due to preexisting surface cracks through which the oxidation process occurred.
Nonetheless, the existence of such open surface cracks, their propagation process and their influence on the poor creep properties of the material under tension should be further investigated.

item.mechanism: Casting inhomogeneity in gravity casting leads to significant grain size variations, causing scattering in mechanical test results compared to the uniform suction-assisted casting.
item.operating_conditions: Room temperature compression and tension testing
item.supporting_observation: Fractography showed significant grain size variation in gravity casting fracture surfaces, whereas suction-assisted casting had uniform grain size; compression results for gravity casting were relatively scattered.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism explains the scattering in compression data but the primary failure mode in tension remains brittle fracture regardless of grain size uniformity.
item.alternatives_considered: None explicitly stated, but the uniformity of suction-assisted casting is presented as preferable.
quotes: This higher degree of scattering may be related to the variation in grain size detected in the gravity casting as opposed to the uniform grain size of the suction-assisted casting.

A fractography study of the broken tension test specimens revealed significant variations in grain size between the different regions of the fracture surface in the case of the gravity casting, as compared to the uniformity of the grain size in the suction-assisted casting.

item.mechanism: The specific distribution of the HCP phase (evenly dispersed vs. grain boundary concentrated) influences the magnitude of hardness increase after HIP.
item.supporting_observation: Suction-assisted casting showed higher hardness (509.1 HV) than gravity casting (437.2 HV) after HIP, correlating with the HCP phase concentration at grain boundaries.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that before HIP, hardness values were statistically equal between the two casting methods.
quotes: The HCP phase that appeared after HIP is evenly dispersed in the matrix of the gravity-assisted casting, while it is concentrated mostly at the grain boundaries in the case of the suction-assisted casting.

As for the materials that underwent HIP, it is clear that the HIP process increased the hardness of both castings. Nevertheless, in the case of the materials that underwent HIP, the hardness of the suction-assisted casting was found to be greater than that of the gravity cast.

item.mechanism: The BCC phase in the as-cast condition is a supercooled phase stabilized by rapid cooling, preventing the formation of the equilibrium HCP phase.
item.supporting_observation: XRD of as-cast samples showed a single BCC phase, while HIP samples showed BCC + HCP, attributed to cooling rates.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism applies specifically to the as-cast state; the thermodynamic stability of the BCC phase at room temperature without the kinetic restriction of rapid cooling is not fully resolved.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors reference Senkov et al. who suggested the BCC phase might be metastable but kinetically restricted.
quotes: In contrast, an HCP phase is not created in the case of the as-cast alloy due to the rapid cooling, resulting in a supercooled BCC phase.

They emphasized that it was not yet known whether the BCC phase is thermodynamically stable at Room Temperature (RT), or whether it is metastable and thus kinetically restricts formation of the low temperature HCP phase due to slow diffusivity.

item.mechanism: Cold rolling and subsequent annealing fundamentally alter the microstructure (grain elongation, deformation bands, texture) and mechanical properties (ductility) compared to the cast/HIP condition.
item.system: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy (86.4% cold rolled and annealed)
item.operating_conditions: 86.4% cold rolling followed by annealing at 800 °C and 1000 °C
item.supporting_observation: Cited literature shows cold-rolled material has tensile ductility of 4.7%, whereas the current study's cast/HIP material is extremely brittle.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism explains the difference between the current study's results and previous literature (Senkov et al.) but does not apply to the as-cast/HIP material studied here.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors contrast the current brittle results with the ductile results of the cold-rolled material to highlight microstructural differences.
quotes: These results, in turn, lead to the conclusion that both the microstructure and the mechanical properties of the HIP'ed material and those of the HIP'ed plus cold rolled material are markedly different.
Cold rolling resulted in an extensive grain elongation, formation of deformation bands within the grains, and development of crystallographic textures that depended on the rolling reduction.
